summary: Redwood AE+SE walked DataScale through Optimize quantization profiles (INT8 and FP8). Main focus: expected latency improvements, token-cost tradeoffs, and measurable impact on downstream quality. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Michael Torres (DataScale CTO), Sana Patel (ML Eng), Ethan Reed (Infra)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20251022-ds-0421

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Jordan Lee from Redwood, i'll kick us off. Priya from our infra/optimize team is here. Michael, Sana, Ethan, thanks for taking the time. quick agenda: run through Optimize's quantization profiles, show INT8 vs FP8 numbers, then discuss pilot scope. sound good?

[00:25] Michael: Sounds good. we mostly want to understand quality impact — our prompts are fairly short but strict on accuracy. also latency, of course.

[00:35] Priya: Great. i'll start with a quick high-level, then show slides and a demo. caveat: some numbers are fabbed for the demo but we'll share the raw bench sheet after.

[00:48] Priya: So, Optimize has pre-made quantization profiles: INT8 conservative, INT8 aggressive, FP8 mixed, FP8 aggressive; they map to different kernels and rounding strategies. INT8 gives you the biggest size/cost reduction but can introduce more numerical drift in some attention heads, FP8 tends to keep quality higher at lower latency than float32 but with slightly higher memory than INT8.

[01:20] Sana: When you say "FP8 mixed", is that block-wise per-layer or per-tensor?

[01:25] Priya: Per-block profiling — we choose per-layer quant format based on sensitivity. it's an automated profiling pass in Optimize that tags sensitive layers to remain higher precision. that's actually one of the key differences vs a dumb full-int8 conversion.

[01:40] Jordan: i'll share the deck real quick — slide 7 has the quality vs latency chart. link: https://redwood.ai/decks/optimize-quant-walk.pdf (note: internal demo link).

[01:55] Priya: Ok, demo time. i'm going to run two requests against the same model: baseline float32 (or bfloat) run on our hosted runtime, INT8-aggressive profile, and FP8-mixed profile. i'll stream the logs and then we'll look at the corpus-level rouge/bleu-ish metrics we computed.

[02:20] [screen share noise]

[02:35] Priya: First run — baseline: p50 token latency 20ms, p95 55ms, throughput 40 reqs/s on this instance. INT8 aggressive: p50 12ms, p95 38ms, throughput 65 reqs/s. FP8 mixed: p50 14ms, p95 42ms, throughput 58 reqs/s.

[03:10] Ethan: Those are impressive. when you say p95, is that end-to-end or just decode loop?

[03:15] Priya: Good q — that's inference-only decode loop, excluding network overhead. for end-to-end we'd add ~5-15ms depending on region.

[03:30] Priya: On quality we ran a 1k prompt eval set (representative of your short-turn QA prompts). baseline (FP32) accuracy 92.1%. INT8-aggressive dropped to 89.6% on that set. FP8-mixed was 91.4%. so you get big latency/cost wins with INT8, but FP8 recovers most quality while still giving large speedups vs FP32.

[04:00] Michael: 2.5% drop is a bit concerning for a product where correctness matters. is there a way to selectively use INT8 for non-critical routes?

[04:10] Jordan: Yes, that's where routing and per-route Optimize profiles come in. you can set the user-facing low-risk routes to INT8 aggressive and keep critical flows on FP8 or even baseline. Redwood routing policies can A/B or canary between profiles.

[04:30] Sana: How deterministic are these differences? like, do INT8 errors show a pattern?

[04:38] Priya: We observed mainly paraphrase/precision loss — numbers and entity recall more than hallucination introductions. but depends on model architecture; for decoder-only models some attention patterns are more fragile. that's why per-layer profiling matters.

[04:55] [15s pause, typing]

[05:15] Priya: quick note on calibration — Optimize runs a micro-calibration pass with a small subset of your prompts to pick per-layer formats and also to output a quality degradation estimate (we gave the 2.5% figure after calibration). that helps tune between INT8/FP8.

[05:35] Ethan: what's the sample size for calibration? we can't leak prod data.

[05:40] Priya: By default it's 200-500 prompts; you can run it on synthetic or on-prem datasets in the pilot. and for privacy you can run profiling in your VPC if you're on Private.

[05:55] Michael: Security wise — KMS, audit logs? we need to know retention and whether the profiling artifacts can be kept customer-side.

[06:05] Jordan: yes, we support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) on Private; audit logs are available in Redwood Console; profiling artifacts can be exported and kept in your S3 or VPC. we'll attach the security pack after this call.

[06:25] Sana: curious about cost math — can you share per-token cost delta?

[06:30] Jordan: high-level: INT8 can be 40-55% cheaper per-token vs baseline, FP8 around 25-40% depending on throughput and batch. we'll include a per-hour instance comparison in the bench sheet.

[06:45] Priya: Also note autoscaling interplay — INT8 reduces memory pressure so you can pack more sessions per GPU; that affects utilization and amortized cost.

[07:00] Michael: For our traffic pattern — short bursts with spiky traffic — what would you recommend? burst capacity or reserved?

[07:10] Jordan: For spikes, Dedicated with burst policies is solid; for initial pilot hosted or Dedicated dev pool. If you want predictability on p95, Dedicated is easier to commit to.

[07:25] [screen flicker]

[07:30] Priya: i pulled up the bench sheet: here's the CSV link (demo): https://redwood.ai/bench/ff-20251022-quant.csv. showing sample prompts, per-prompt delta, and token-cost calc.

[07:45] Sana: looks good. in your csv, i see a column "sensi_score" — what is that?

[07:50] Priya: sensitivity score is per-layer sensitivity flagged by the profiler — higher means more likely to degrade with int8. we use it to choose mixed FP8 for those layers.

[08:05] Michael: let's talk about pilot design. we want to run both INT8 and FP8, maybe route 10% of traffic to each and compare production metrics for 2 weeks. can Redwood support that split and metrics comparison?

[08:20] Jordan: yes — we can do a canary roll using per-route policies and provide instrumentation in Console for cost, latency, and a simple quality proxy (token-level diffs and a set of golden prompts). Priya: we also support automated regression alerts tied to eval sets.

[08:40] Priya: i can template the pilot: sample set, calibration run, three-model rollout (baseline, FP8, INT8), rolling canary @10/10/80 or similar, daily summary.

[09:00] Ethan: what's required from our side infra-wise? we use GCP, VPC peering, and strict egress rules.

[09:08] Jordan: For Private deployment, we can provide VPC connectors and convoy an on-prem image; for Hosted Shared you need to allow outbound to our endpoint — we'll send network docs. if you want profiling kept in your VPC, recommend Private.

[09:30] Michael: any regulatory or SOC2 stuff tied to the Optimize profiling?

[09:36] Jordan: same compliance posture applies — profiling metadata is not model secrets, but we treat it as customer-controlled artifacts with retention settings and encryption at rest. we'll attach SOC2 and ISO docs.

[09:50] [short demo continues]

[10:15] Priya: quick deep dive: FP8 uses a per-block exponent biasing trick; in practice this means smaller dynamic range than bfloat but enough for most transformer matmuls. INT8 needs requantization for MLP layers which is where we see biggest loss if done naively.

[10:45] Sana: do you mutate the model or is it a runtime quant path?

[10:48] Priya: runtime — we produce a memory-backed quantized kernel at load-time; model artifacts can be stored as a quantized variant if you want reproducible artifacts for Dedicated/Private.

[11:05] Michael: can we pin version and revert quickly if we see regression?

[11:08] Jordan: yes, Console supports model version pinning and rollback, with canary and traffic split options.

[11:20] [20s pause, unrelated side conversation, background noise]

[11:45] Priya: here's a small example prompt where INT8 changed an entity: prompt about customer "Acme Corp" looked like "Acme corp" but downstream tagging broke. FP8 preserved the entity. small but product-impacting.

[12:05] Michael: good to know. we have downstream entity extractors so that could blow up. maybe route entity-heavy flows to FP8.

[12:20] Jordan: exactly — that's the recommendation. route-by-intent is a common approach.

[12:35] Sana: logging — do you provide diffs between baseline and quant outputs?

[12:40] Priya: we provide token-diff tooling in Console for your golden-set evals; you can also stream raw outputs into your logger if you enable that.

[12:55] Ethan: latency SLO objective: p95 under 90ms end-to-end. doable with INT8?

[13:02] Priya: with regional hosting and our prefix caching we usually hit p95 ~40-60ms decode plus network. INT8 gives you margin to fit under 90ms if network is okay. but Dedicated with pinned resources is better evidence to meet strict SLO.

[13:25] Michael: what's the expected work to integrate? can the SEs help with the calibration?

[13:30] Jordan: yes — SE-led pilot: profiling, initial calibrations, and weekly check-ins. Priya: we usually do a 2-week pilot with 1 week of calibration/benching and 1 week of production canary.

[13:45] [chat ping noise]

[14:00] Michael: can you email the proposed pilot template and the bench CSV?

[14:05] Jordan: yes, will do. action: Jordan send pilot template + pricing + bench CSV.

[14:12] Priya: one last note: mixed FP8 profiles often give best tradeoff for QA-heavy workloads; INT8 for high throughput non-critical which do a lot of token generation.

[14:30] Michael: ok that makes sense. on pricing, we'll need a ballpark for pilot costs and a committed Dedicated price if we go that route.

[14:40] Jordan: we'll include both. also note the Optimize credits for first pilot.

[14:50] Sana: quick question on model variants — we use OSS transformer models and a few custom fine-tunes. does profiling handle fine-tuned weights?

[14:58] Priya: yes, profiling runs on your actual weights. we recommend running on the fine-tune to get accurate sensitivity.

[15:10] [wrap-up]

[15:15] Jordan: recap: Priya will share quant profiles and bench CSV; Jordan will send pricing + pilot template + security docs; DataScale will provide sample prompts and traffic patterns. follow-up 30m tech check-in next week.

[15:30] Michael: thanks, good session.

[15:35] Jordan: thanks all.

[15:40] [meeting ends]

Notes: transcript contains occasional ASR errors and speaker attribution approximations. links are demo placeholders.
